name: Mwakai
confidence_why: Barlow's 2020 sketch, the only description of Mwakai, states that stress is not phonemic and gives no placement rule, and his 2020 Pondi sketch and 2023 Ulwa grammar say nothing about Mwakai stress, so the record rests on one first-hand source with nothing against it.
catalog_citation: Barlow, Russell. 2020. Notes on Mwakai, East Sepik Province, Papua New Guinea. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 38: 37-99.
catalog_locator: §2 'Phonetics and phonology', p. 46 (stress statement; the paragraph begins at the foot of p. 45); §2.2.1-2.2.5, pp. 53-55 (vowel allophony 'when unstressed': …
catalog_quote: There are 18 phonemes in Mwakai, consisting of 12 consonants and 6 vowels. In terms of its phonemes, Mwakai is similar to its two closest sister languages, Ulwa and Pondi. The phonetic realization of some of these phonemes, however, differs from what is found in Ulwa and Pondi. Stress in Mwakai is not phonemic. Nor is there phonemic tone, nor are other suprasegmental phonemic distinctions made in the language. ... The high front unrounded vowel /i/ is rarely pronounced as the cardinal vowel [i], but is rather more often realized as the lax vowel [ɪ] or as the high central vowel [ɨ], especially when unstressed. ... The low central unrounded vowel /a/ is generally pronounced as [a], but it may be pronounced a bit higher, as [ə], especially when unstressed and in word-final position.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation and all 'when unstressed' allophony sentences are verbatim in the publisher PDF we hold at the stated pages (p.46; pp.53-55). (2) The source is a 2020 fieldwork-based grammar sketch by the only linguist who has described Mwakai; Glottolog has n=1 descriptive refs and Barlow's own 2023 Ulwa grammar (downloaded, p.25) cites it as the Mwakai description of record; ORCID shows no later Mwakai work. (3) Two open Barlow works downloaded now (Ulwa grammar 2023; Pondi sketch 2020) are silent on Mwakai stress; the Pondi sketch only gives sister-language context (non-phonemic, slight penult preference in disyllables), which cannot license a position coding for Mwakai. (4) 'undetermined' with the primary-stress rule noting phonetic but non-contrastive stress is exactly what the source supports; nothing better exists, so no reclassification and no evidence-grade change. sources.quote: On the closest sister language Pondi, not Mwakai: 'Stress in Pondi is not phonemic. In single-word utterances, disyllabic words may receive stress either on the ultima or on the penult, although there is perhaps a slight preference for penultimate (trochaic) stress.' Nothing on Mwakai stress.
